lesson.title: When a System Has Somewhere to Land
lesson.summary: A consistent system is one that has at least one solution, meaning its graphs share at least one common point, whether that is a single intersection or an entire overlapping line.
lesson.body:
A system of equations is called consistent when there is at least one ordered pair that makes every equation in it true. That is the broad, umbrella case: a consistent system might have exactly one solution, or it might have infinitely many, but what it can never have is zero. The word describes the presence of an answer, not how many answers there are, which is an important distinction to keep straight as the vocabulary around systems keeps growing. Think of consistent as answering only the yes-or-no question of whether the system can be solved at all, saving the question of how many solutions exist for later.

This label connects directly to the idea of a solution of a system covered earlier. To decide whether a system is consistent, you look for at least one ordered pair that checks out in every equation, using the same substitution process used to verify any candidate solution. If such a pair exists, however many there turn out to be, the system earns the label consistent. If you can produce even one verified solution, the classification question is already settled, regardless of how that solution was found, whether by graphing, substitution, or elimination. It does not matter whether the pair was easy or hard to find; only its existence, once verified, decides the classification.

Consider the system x + y = 5 and x - y = 1. Adding the two equations cancels y: (x + y) + (x - y) = 5 + 1, so 2x = 6, giving x = 3. Substituting back into x + y = 5 gives 3 + y = 5, so y = 2. Check both originals: 3 + 2 = 5 matches the first equation, and 3 - 2 = 1 matches the second. Since the ordered pair (3, 2) satisfies both equations, at least one solution exists, and the system is consistent. Notice that finding this single verified pair was enough to prove consistency; no further searching for other solutions was required to answer the classification question.

Geometrically, consistency shows up in two different pictures. Two lines that cross at a single point share exactly one common point, so that system is consistent. Two equations that describe the exact same line, drawn on top of each other, share every point on that line, so that system is consistent too, just in a more extreme way. What both pictures have in common is that the lines actually touch somewhere, which is the entire meaning of consistent; how much they touch, at one point or along the whole line, is a separate question answered by the next two sections.

The next two sections split this broad category in half. A consistent system with exactly one shared point is called independent, while a consistent system whose equations describe the same line, sharing infinitely many points, is called dependent. Both are still consistent, since both have at least one solution. The opposite situation, where the lines never meet at all, produces an inconsistent system, examined right after this one, in which no ordered pair can ever satisfy both equations, no matter how far the lines are extended in either direction.
